sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9421 — HTTP Message Signatures
sources.role: HTTP covered-component, signature-base, key-material and application-policy contract
verified_facts: HTTP Message Signatures create and verify signatures or MACs over selected components of an HTTP message.
The covered-components set and its order determine the signature base reconstructed by signer and verifier.
A safe application profile must define required covered components, signature parameters, algorithms, key material and verification requirements.
semantic_limits: A valid signature proves integrity or authenticity only for the components actually covered; uncovered content remains outside the proof.
HTTP Message Signatures do not directly cover message content unless an appropriate digest component is included and verified.
Signature success does not establish terrain accuracy, exact parcel geometry, vertical datum, units or the truth of a height claim.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 7515 — JSON Web Signature (JWS)
sources.role: JWS protected-header, payload, algorithm, key identifier and signing-input contract
verified_facts: JWS represents content protected with digital signatures or MACs using JSON-based structures.
The JWS Signing Input binds the protected header and payload, while Compact and JSON serializations share the same cryptographic basis.
The alg parameter identifies the cryptographic algorithm and must be understood; kid is only a hint for selecting a key.
semantic_limits: A verified JWS establishes integrity for its signing input, not the authority or scientific correctness of the payload.
A kid, jku, jwk or certificate reference must not be accepted as trusted key identity without independent policy and retrieval validation.
JWS success must not create a parcel-height row unless source bytes, exact geometry, CRS, vertical datum, units, method and provenance also pass.

sources.name: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
sources.role: issuer, holder, verifier, credential subject, status, validity and claim-reliance contract
verified_facts: A verifiable credential expresses claims made by an issuer and is processed by holders and verifiers.
Verification evaluates whether a credential or presentation is authentic and current and whether its securing mechanism and status checks succeed.
The Recommendation explicitly states that verifiability does not imply the truth of the claims; relying parties apply their own policies.
semantic_limits: Issuer authenticity and credential currency do not prove that a parcel-height claim is scientifically or cadastral-correct.
Credential status, validity period, type and schema conformance are distinct from source-byte, geometry and measurement validation.
A credential claim must remain support-only until the exact distribution, method, units, vertical datum and execution receipts are independently verified.

sources.name: Verifiable Credential Data Integrity 1.0
sources.role: data-integrity proof, cryptographic suite, verification method, proof purpose and proof-chain contract
verified_facts: Data Integrity proofs provide authenticity and integrity mechanisms for constrained digital documents using cryptography.
A proof contains attributes and parameters required for verification, and proof purpose states the intended use of the proof.
Verifiers must ensure that proof purpose matches the intended use; proof sets and chains require their defined verification processing.
semantic_limits: A cryptographic proof is not proof that the underlying measurement or claim is true.
Proof-purpose or proof-chain validity does not replace key-trust policy, source authority, exact bytes or measurement provenance.
A proof covering a credential must not be reused as an F-host recovery, download, numeric-sampling or port-8012 execution receipt.
